ch-alcohol-01.question: Under Art. 31 para. 2 SVG, a person is deemed unfit to drive (fahrunfähig) if alcohol, narcotics, or medication leave them without the necessary physical and mental capacity. What does the law additionally state?

options.a: Only a proven alcohol level of 0.3 per mille or more makes someone unfit to drive
options.b: Any other reason ('aus anderen Gründen', e.g. exhaustion) lacking that capacity also makes someone unfit to drive
options.c: Unfitness only applies once police have formally established intoxication
options.d: Only narcotics, not medication, can cause unfitness to drive

ch-alcohol-01.explanation: Art. 31 para. 2 SVG is deliberately open-ended: 'alcohol, narcotics or medication, or for other reasons'. This catches any cause of reduced fitness to drive, including exhaustion or illness, without reference to any alcohol figure. German law (§ 315c StGB) lists causes more narrowly ('mental or physical defects', alcohol, intoxicants); the Swiss catch-all clause is broader.

ch-alcohol-02.question: Under Art. 55 para. 1 SVG, drivers and road users involved in an accident can be required to take a breath alcohol test. What applies in Switzerland to ordering this check?

options.a: It can be required during a routine traffic stop even without any suspicion of impairment
options.b: It may only be ordered where there are visible signs of intoxication
options.c: It is only permitted after a traffic accident causing personal injury
options.d: A prior judicial order is required

ch-alcohol-02.explanation: The statutory wording ('may be required') sets no threshold of suspicion; Swiss police may run systematic, suspicion-free breath checks at traffic stops. Germany also permits checks without cause, but that authority typically sits in state police law rather than in the StVG itself; Switzerland regulates this centrally and explicitly in the SVG.

ch-alcohol-03.question: From what blood alcohol concentration does Swiss law treat someone as being 'angetrunken' (intoxicated), punishable under Art. 91 para. 1 lit. a SVG only as an Übertretung (fine)?

options.a: 0.3 per mille
options.b: 0.5 per mille
options.c: 0.8 per mille
options.d: 1.1 per mille

ch-alcohol-03.explanation: The basic threshold is 0.5 per mille, the same as Germany's fine-only limit under § 24a StVG. The difference appears at the next tier: in Switzerland the offence already turns into a criminal Vergehen (custodial or monetary penalty) from 0.8 per mille, not only from 1.1 per mille as under Germany's absolute-unfitness offence.

ch-alcohol-04.question: From what 'qualified' blood alcohol concentration does driving under the influence in Switzerland become a Vergehen under Art. 91 para. 2 lit. a SVG, punishable by up to three years' imprisonment or a monetary penalty - regardless of any actually observed impairment?

options.a: 0.5 per mille
options.b: 0.3 per mille combined with proven signs of impairment
options.c: 0.8 per mille
options.d: 1.1 per mille

ch-alcohol-04.explanation: The 'qualified' threshold is 0.8 per mille - from this value a Vergehen is assumed automatically, regardless of impairment. In Germany the comparable threshold for absolute unfitness (§ 316 StGB) is 1.1 per mille; relative unfitness only applies from 0.3 per mille together with actual signs of impairment. Switzerland therefore draws the line into criminal territory considerably earlier.

ch-alcohol-05.question: In Swiss traffic-enforcement practice, which breath alcohol value corresponds to the qualified blood alcohol threshold of 0.8 per mille?
ch-alcohol-05.explanation: Breath alcohol concentration (mg/l of breath) and blood alcohol concentration (per mille) are two different measurements and must not be equated. Under Swiss practice, 0.25 mg/l of breath corresponds to the basic 0.5 per mille threshold, while 0.40 mg/l corresponds to the qualified 0.8 per mille threshold. A breath figure of '0.8' simply does not exist in the Swiss system - confusing mg/l with per mille is a classic mistake.

ch-alcohol-06.question: Holders of a probationary licence (Neulenker) are subject to a strict alcohol ban ('zero tolerance') under Art. 2a VRV. According to the statutory wording, what blood alcohol value may they reach at most before the ban applies?

options.a: 0.0 per mille (an absolute, literal zero)
options.b: 0.10 per mille
options.c: 0.5 per mille
options.d: 0.05 per mille

ch-alcohol-06.explanation: Switzerland's 'zero tolerance', despite its name, is not a literal zero but sits at 0.10 per mille (or 0.05 mg/l breath alcohol). This is an important contrast with Germany: there, novice drivers in their probationary period and drivers under 21 face a genuine 0.0 per mille limit under § 24c StVG - any detectable trace of alcohol is already prohibited.

ch-alcohol-07.question: The 0.10 per mille limit under Art. 2a VRV is not limited to novice drivers. Which group is also explicitly covered?

options.a: Professional drivers of trucks over 3.5 t and driving instructors while giving instruction
options.b: All motorcyclists, regardless of how long they have held a licence
options.c: Only taxi drivers in major cities
options.d: Only persons under 21, regardless of licence type

ch-alcohol-07.explanation: Art. 2a para. 1 VRV lists, alongside novice drivers, professional passenger and goods transport (including trucks over 3.5 t and dangerous-goods transport), driving instructors while teaching, and accompanying persons on learner drives. Germany's equivalent under § 24c StVG, by contrast, is tied purely to age (under 21) or probationary status, with no comparable occupation-based zero-value category in the same provision.

ch-alcohol-08.question: A probationary licence holder commits their first alcohol-related offence during the three-year probation period, resulting in a licence withdrawal. What happens to their probation period?

options.a: The probation period is extended by one year
options.b: The probationary licence is immediately and permanently annulled
options.c: The probation period is unaffected; only a fine follows
options.d: Points are added to a central points register, and probation continues unchanged

ch-alcohol-08.explanation: Under Art. 15a SVG, a first offence during the three-year probation period that leads to a licence withdrawal extends probation by one year. Only a second such offence leads to annulment (see the next question). Germany has no points-register equivalent within its probation period itself; there, a traffic offence typically extends the two-year probation by two years and triggers a remedial seminar, without the Swiss cascading model that ends in annulment.

ch-alcohol-09.question: What happens if a probationary licence holder commits a second offence leading to a licence withdrawal during the (possibly already extended) probation period?

options.a: Probation is extended by a further year
options.b: The probationary licence is annulled; a new learner's permit is required to start again
options.c: Only a stricter fine schedule applies
options.d: The licence is withdrawn for exactly three months, after which it automatically becomes a full licence

ch-alcohol-09.explanation: A second offence during probation that leads to a licence withdrawal results, under Art. 35a VZV, in annulment of the probationary licence. To drive again afterwards, the person must apply for a new learner's permit, undergo a traffic-psychology assessment, and retake the driving test. A system this drastic - resetting everything to zero on a second offence - has no counterpart in German driving-licence law.

ch-alcohol-10.question: Driving with a qualified breath or blood alcohol concentration counts as a serious violation (schwere Widerhandlung) under Art. 16c SVG. How is the warning-based licence withdrawal for such serious violations structured?

options.a: As a points system, where reaching eight points automatically triggers withdrawal
options.b: As a cascading system with statutory minimum withdrawal periods that escalate on a repeat serious violation (e.g. at least two years, and indefinitely on further relapse)
options.c: The licence is always withdrawn for life on the very first incident
options.d: Switzerland has no warning-based withdrawal at all, only criminal sanctions

ch-alcohol-10.explanation: The SVG has no points system comparable to Germany's Fahreignungsregister (the Flensburg register, with withdrawal from eight points). Instead, Art. 16c SVG sets out a cascading system of fixed statutory minimum withdrawal periods: at least two years for a serious violation involving genuine endangerment, escalating further up to an indefinite withdrawal on relapse within the statutory time windows. The duration follows directly from the statute, not from a points tally.

ch-priority-01.question: Two cars approach an unmarked, equal-ranking intersection at the same time from streets that cross at right angles. Under Swiss law, who has the Vortritt (right of way)?

options.a: The vehicle coming from the right
options.b: Whichever vehicle reached the intersection first
options.c: The larger or heavier vehicle
options.d: Both must stop and signal to each other by hand

ch-priority-01.explanation: SVG Art. 36 para. 2: at an unsignalled intersection, the vehicle coming from the right has the Vortritt. This matches the outcome of the German 'rechts vor links' rule (§ 8 StVO) - but Switzerland's official legal term for this right is 'Vortritt', not 'Vorfahrt'.

ch-priority-02.question: A main road (Hauptstrasse) changes direction at a junction, and minor side roads join it at the same point. A driver leaves the main road to turn into a side road. Whom must they yield to?

options.a: Only oncoming traffic on the main road
options.b: All vehicles from every joining road equally, as under rechts-vor-links
options.c: No one, because they are coming from the main road
options.d: Only vehicles coming from the right out of the side road

ch-priority-02.explanation: VRV Art. 15 para. 1: when the main road bends and side roads join at the same spot, a driver turning off the main road only has to yield to oncoming traffic on the main road - not to everyone under a general rechts-vor-links, as a German driver might expect. German StVO has no directly equivalent special rule for such 'kinked' priority roads.

ch-priority-03.question: Two roads, each signed «Stop» or «Kein Vortritt» (no priority), join a priority road at the same point. What rule applies between the two waiting vehicles themselves?

options.a: Right-of-way from the right applies between them
options.b: Both may enter simultaneously once the priority road is clear
options.c: The vehicle on the «Stop» road always has priority over the one on the «Kein Vortritt» road
options.d: Whichever vehicle arrived first goes first

ch-priority-03.explanation: VRV Art. 15 para. 2: where two or more roads signed «Stop» or «Kein Vortritt» join a priority road at the same point, right-of-way from the right applies among the waiting drivers themselves. Which of the two signs each one carries does not matter between them - a detail German StVO does not spell out this explicitly for junctions with several give-way/stop signs.

ch-priority-04.question: A driver exits a factory driveway, crossing a pavement, onto a main road. What does VRV Art. 15 para. 3 require?

options.a: They must always yield to all users of the road and of the pavement
options.b: They have priority because they are entering a public road from private property
options.c: Ordinary rechts-vor-links applies, as at a normal intersection
options.d: They may enter as long as no vehicle is immediately visible

ch-priority-04.explanation: VRV Art. 15 para. 3: anyone driving out of a factory, yard or garage exit, a field path, cycle path, car park, filling station and the like, or across a pavement onto a road, must always yield to that road's users - including pedestrians on the pavement. There is no priority of any kind here, broadly similar to the German duty on 'entering and moving off' (StVO § 10), though set out as its own separate and more detailed rule.

ch-priority-05.question: A tram approaches an intersection at the same time as a car coming from the right. Under SVG Art. 38, who has the Vortritt?

options.a: The tram, always
options.b: The car, because it is coming from the right
options.c: The tram, but only if it sounds a warning signal
options.d: Ordinary rechts-vor-links applies, as between two cars

ch-priority-05.explanation: SVG Art. 38 para. 1: the tram's track must be kept clear and it must always be given the Vortritt, regardless of which direction it comes from. This goes noticeably further than the German rule, where trams usually have priority but do not unconditionally override every other right-of-way rule.

ch-priority-06.question: A driver wants to enter a roundabout (Kreisel). What does VRV Art. 41b para. 1 require?

options.a: They must slow down and yield to vehicles already circulating that are approaching from the left
options.b: They have priority if they are entering from the right
options.c: They must come to a complete stop before entering
options.d: They may enter as long as they signal in time

ch-priority-06.explanation: VRV Art. 41b para. 1: before entering, the driver must slow down and yield to vehicles already circulating and approaching from the left. The outcome matches Germany's roundabout rule (sign 215) - unlike ordinary 'right before left', here it is clearly the circulating traffic that has priority, not vehicles entering from the right.

ch-priority-07.question: On a steep mountain road, two similar vehicles (e.g. two cars) cannot pass each other. Under VRV Art. 38 para. 1, which one must reverse?

options.a: The downhill vehicle, unless the other one is close to a passing place
options.b: The uphill vehicle, because it is slower
options.c: Whichever of the two is lighter
options.d: Ordinary rechts-vor-links applies, so the one coming from the right stays put

ch-priority-07.explanation: VRV Art. 38 para. 1: if similar vehicles cannot pass each other on a steep or mountain road, the downhill vehicle must generally reverse - so the uphill vehicle effectively has priority. German StVO has no such dedicated mountain-road rule at all; only the general duty of mutual consideration applies there.

ch-priority-08.question: On a mountain postal road (Bergpoststrasse), passing or overtaking becomes difficult. What must other drivers do under VRV Art. 38 para. 3?

options.a: Follow the signs and instructions given by the drivers of scheduled-service vehicles (the Postauto)
options.b: Nothing special - just the ordinary mountain-road passing rule
options.c: Only give way to the Postauto if it sounds its horn
options.d: Stop and wave the Postauto past, but otherwise carry on as normal

ch-priority-08.explanation: VRV Art. 38 para. 3: on mountain postal roads, when passing or overtaking is difficult, drivers must follow the signs and instructions given by drivers of scheduled-service vehicles - in practice, above all the yellow Postauto. The Postauto can actively direct traffic this way. Germany has no comparable statutory special status for a scheduled bus on mountain roads.

ch-priority-09.question: A driver approaches a «Stop» sign (3.01). There is no vehicle visible on the road they are approaching, for as far as they can see. What does SSV Art. 36 para. 1 require?

options.a: They must stop anyway and grant the right of way
options.b: They may drive through if the road is visibly clear
options.c: They only need to slow down, as at a «Kein Vortritt» sign
options.d: They only need to stop if police are present

ch-priority-09.explanation: SSV Art. 36 para. 1: the «Stop» sign requires the driver to stop and yield the right of way, regardless of whether any traffic is visible. This matches the German Stop rule (sign 206), but in Switzerland it is set out as its own distinct duty, clearly separated from the «Kein Vortritt» (no-priority) sign (3.02), which does not require a mandatory stop.

ch-priority-10.question: A road is marked with the «Hauptstrasse» sign (3.03, a yellow diamond). Under SSV Art. 37 para. 1, what effect does this sign have at the intersections that follow?

options.a: The statutory right-of-way-from-the-right is cancelled, and the main road has priority
options.b: Ordinary rechts-vor-links still applies; the sign is purely informational
options.c: Only vehicles over 3.5 t benefit from the indicated priority
options.d: The sign only applies outside built-up areas and has no effect within them

ch-priority-10.explanation: SSV Art. 37 para. 1: the «Hauptstrasse» sign marks priority roads and cancels the statutory right-of-way-from-the-right at the intersections that follow. In effect this matches the German priority-road sign (Zeichen 306) - except the Swiss diamond is solid yellow, while the German equivalent is white with a yellow diamond inside.

ch-signs-01.question: You are driving on a road signed «Hauptstrasse» (main road, sign 3.03) in Switzerland. Before a minor side road, the sign is not repeated. What is the state of your right of way at that junction?

options.a: You still have priority - the sign may be omitted at insignificant junctions without the main road losing its status
options.b: Without a repeated sign, right-before-left applies automatically, as at an ordinary German junction
options.c: The main road's priority automatically lapses after any junction where the sign is not repeated
options.d: You only keep priority if a Stop sign is additionally posted on the side road

ch-signs-01.explanation: Art. 37(2) SSV allows the main-road sign to be omitted at insignificant junctions, yet priority continues unchanged. In Germany the priority-road sign (Zeichen 306) is instead reposted at nearly every junction, so a missing sign there would raise doubt about continued priority - in Switzerland it is not grounds to assume right-before-left.

ch-signs-02.question: What is the background colour of the Swiss «Autobahn» (motorway) sign (4.01) marking the start of a motorway?

options.a: Green
options.b: Blue, like the equivalent sign in Germany
options.c: Yellow
options.d: Red with a white symbol

ch-signs-02.explanation: Since 1972, Swiss motorway signs and guide signs have been green, to set them apart from what were then uniformly blue direction signs. Germany (and France), by contrast, use blue for the motorway - so a German driver should not mistake a green Swiss sign for a minor road.

ch-signs-03.question: In Switzerland, a blue guide sign (direction/distance sign) points the way to which category of road?

options.a: A Hauptstrasse (main road)
options.b: A motorway (Autobahn)
options.c: A Nebenstrasse (secondary road)
options.d: An Autostrasse (expressway)

ch-signs-03.explanation: Under Art. 51 SSV, guide signs for main roads are blue, for motorways green, and for secondary roads white. This is the exact reverse of the German convention, where blue marks the motorway and yellow marks federal roads (Bundesstrassen) - a German driver who reflexively equates blue with the motorway would head the wrong way in Switzerland.

ch-signs-04.question: You are driving a passenger car (up to 3.5 t) on a Swiss national road of class I or II (motorway or expressway). What fee applies?

options.a: A fixed annual fee of CHF 40 (the vignette), regardless of distance driven or which class of national road you use
options.b: A distance-based toll, as is common in some other countries
options.c: No fee - national roads are free of charge for cars in Switzerland
options.d: A fee only on class-I motorways, not on class-II expressways

ch-signs-04.explanation: Art. 2 f. NSAG levies the fee uniformly on national roads I and II, and Art. 6 sets the amount at CHF 40 per year, regardless of mileage. Germany currently has no general motorway toll for passenger cars - assuming no fee at all applies would leave a driver without a valid vignette in Switzerland, and liable to a fine.

ch-signs-05.question: Under what condition may a double safety line (sign 6.02, two solid white lines) be marked in Switzerland instead of a single safety line?

options.a: On roads with at least three lanes, or, where a particular safety need exists, also on two-lane roads
options.b: Always outside built-up areas, regardless of the number of lanes
options.c: Only on motorways
options.d: Only inside a 30 km/h zone

ch-signs-05.explanation: Art. 73(2) SSV ties the double safety line to a minimum of three lanes, or a particular safety need on two-lane roads - an explicit lane-count threshold that German marking practice does not define in the same way.

ch-signs-06.question: Ahead of you a broken-down vehicle blocks so much of the lane that there is not enough room to pass without crossing a solid safety line. May you cross the safety line?

options.a: Yes, but only for a compelling reason such as an insurmountable obstacle, when waiting is not reasonable
options.b: Yes, crossing a safety line to overtake is generally allowed as long as no oncoming traffic is near
options.c: No, crossing is prohibited without exception, even to get around an obstacle
options.d: Yes, but only with hazard lights on for the whole manoeuvre

ch-signs-06.explanation: Art. 73(6) SSV prohibits crossing a safety line in principle; case law allows an exception only for a compelling reason, such as a genuine obstacle. Germany's equivalent lane-boundary line (Zeichen 295) is applied somewhat more permissively in practice, for instance when overtaking cyclists - Switzerland's narrow 'compelling reason' standard leaves less room.

ch-signs-07.question: In Switzerland, what distinguishes the guide line (Leitlinie, broken white; 6.03) from the safety line (Sicherheitslinie, solid white; 6.01)?

options.a: The guide line may be crossed to overtake when visibility is sufficient; the safety line must not be crossed as a rule
options.b: Both lines prohibit crossing to the same extent
options.c: The safety line may be crossed provided you accelerate quickly enough
options.d: The guide line is purely decorative and carries no legal meaning

ch-signs-07.explanation: Art. 73(1) and (3) SSV mirror the principle familiar from Germany: broken lines (guide lines) permit crossing, solid lines (safety lines) generally do not. A driver who knows the German system can carry it over almost unchanged here.

ch-signs-08.question: According to Art. 22b SSV, what is the speed limit in a signed Swiss «Begegnungszone» (encounter zone)?

options.a: 20 km/h - a specific figure fixed in the ordinance
options.b: Walking pace with no fixed number, as in the German traffic-calmed zone (verkehrsberuhigter Bereich)
options.c: 30 km/h
options.d: No speed limit, only a general duty of consideration

ch-signs-08.explanation: Art. 22b SSV explicitly names 20 km/h and gives pedestrians and users of similar wheeled devices priority, as long as they do not unnecessarily obstruct vehicles. German traffic law instead uses the undefined term 'walking pace' for the comparable traffic-calmed zone, with no fixed figure - Switzerland is more precise here.

ch-signs-09.question: According to Art. 36(8) SSV, at what distance outside a built-up area must a «Stop» sign be pre-announced when it exceptionally cancels a main road's priority?

options.a: 150 to 250 metres
options.b: 50 to 100 metres
options.c: There is no obligation to pre-announce it
options.d: At least 500 metres

ch-signs-09.explanation: Art. 36(8) SSV requires advance warning at 150-250 metres outside built-up areas (about 50 metres inside them) whenever a Stop sign exceptionally interrupts a priority road. German road traffic law does not fix a comparable metre range for such advance warning directly in the ordinance itself, leaving the detail to administrative guidance.

ch-signs-10.question: In Switzerland, what distinguishes the «Stop» sign (3.01) from the «Kein Vortritt» (give way) sign (3.02)?

options.a: A «Stop» sign always requires a complete stop; the give-way sign only requires stopping if priority actually has to be yielded
options.b: Both signs always require a complete stop, regardless of traffic
options.c: The give-way sign applies only to trucks and buses
options.d: The Stop sign may only be posted outside built-up areas

ch-signs-10.explanation: Art. 36(1) SSV always requires a full stop at a Stop sign, while Art. 36(2) requires only yielding priority at the give-way sign, with no mandatory stop when the road is clear. This matches, in principle, the German distinction between Zeichen 206 ('Stop. Yield.') and Zeichen 205 ('Yield.') - the logic carries over unchanged.

ch-speed-01.question: On a Swiss Autobahn (motorway) under good conditions with no sign showing a different figure, what is the general speed limit?

options.a: There is no general limit, unrestricted driving as on unlimited stretches of German Autobahnen
options.b: 120 km/h
options.c: 130 km/h, as recommended on many German Autobahn sections
options.d: 140 km/h

ch-speed-01.explanation: VRV Art. 4a para. 1(d) sets the general Autobahn speed limit at 120 km/h, often also posted by sign. Unlike Germany, which has stretches with no general speed limit (only a non-binding recommended speed, Richtgeschwindigkeit, of 130 km/h under StVO § 3), Switzerland has no unlimited motorway anywhere: 120 km/h is the nationwide hard ceiling.

ch-speed-02.question: You are driving outside built-up areas on an ordinary rural road with no special signage. What is the general speed limit?

options.a: 100 km/h, as is common on German rural roads
options.b: 90 km/h
options.c: 80 km/h
options.d: 70 km/h

ch-speed-02.explanation: VRV Art. 4a para. 1(b) sets 80 km/h as the general limit outside built-up areas (excluding motorways/expressways). This is the sharp contrast with Germany, where the default limit outside built-up areas is 100 km/h absent other signs (StVO § 3). A German driver who reflexively drives at 100 is 20 km/h over the Swiss limit.

ch-speed-03.question: You are driving on a Swiss Autostrasse (expressway, marked with the 'Autostrasse' sign) — a road category between an ordinary rural road and a motorway that Germany does not have. What is the general speed limit there?

options.a: 100 km/h
options.b: 80 km/h, the same as on ordinary roads outside built-up areas
options.c: 120 km/h, the same as on the motorway
options.d: 90 km/h

ch-speed-03.explanation: VRV Art. 4a para. 1(c) sets Autostrassen (expressways) at 100 km/h — a distinct middle category between a rural road (80) and a motorway (120). Germany also has a concept of Kraftfahrstrassen but does not give them their own generic speed tier (the general 100 km/h outside-built-up-area default or specific signage usually applies); Switzerland's dedicated 100 km/h rule for this category is a rule to learn specifically.

ch-speed-04.question: The posted speed limit outside built-up areas is 80 km/h, but there is dense fog with visibility of only 30 metres. What does SVG Art. 32 para. 1 require?

options.a: 80 km/h may still be used fully as long as no new sign is posted
options.b: Up to 100 km/h is fine, since fog does not change the road surface
options.c: Speed is irrelevant as long as the low-beam headlights are on
options.d: Speed must be adapted to the visibility conditions, well below 80 km/h

ch-speed-04.explanation: SVG Art. 32 para. 1 requires speed to always be adapted to the circumstances, in particular visibility — a posted limit is only ever a ceiling, never an entitlement to drive it in any weather. This mirrors StVO § 3 para. 1 in Germany in principle; the real contrast lies in the absolute limit values (see other questions), not in this adaptation duty itself.

ch-speed-05.question: You drive into a residential area marked with the 'Tempo-30-Zone' sign (SSV Art. 22a). What speed limit applies there?

options.a: 20 km/h, as in a Begegnungszone (encounter zone)
options.b: 30 km/h
options.c: 50 km/h, unless children are visible
options.d: The zone is only advisory, 50 km/h remains permitted

ch-speed-05.explanation: SSV Art. 22a makes 30 km/h binding on roads marked with the 'Tempo-30-Zone' sign. Germany's equivalent zone under StVO § 45 works similarly as a binding limit; the difference lies more in Switzerland regulating it as its own, nationally uniform sign category rather than a purely local order.

ch-speed-06.question: You are driving through a street marked with the 'Begegnungszone' (encounter zone) sign under SSV Art. 22b. What applies to speed and right-of-way there?

options.a: A maximum of 20 km/h, and pedestrians and users of vehicle-like devices may use the whole surface and have right-of-way
options.b: A maximum of 30 km/h, but pedestrians have no right-of-way over vehicles
options.c: A maximum of 20 km/h, but pedestrians may only walk on the pavement
options.d: The normal built-up-area limit of 50 km/h applies

ch-speed-06.explanation: SSV Art. 22b sets the Begegnungszone limit at 20 km/h and gives pedestrians and users of vehicle-like devices (e.g. kick scooters) the right to use the entire road surface, with right-of-way over vehicles. German law has no directly equivalent statutory zone concept with a fixed 20 km/h limit and explicit whole-surface pedestrian priority; its closest analogue, the verkehrsberuhigter Bereich under the StVO, only demands walking pace without a defined km/h figure.

ch-speed-07.question: Inside built-up areas the general speed limit is 50 km/h. From what amount over the limit does it automatically become a Raser offence under SVG Art. 90 para. 4?

options.a: From 30 km/h over the limit
options.b: From 50 km/h over the limit
options.c: From 60 km/h over the limit
options.d: Only from 80 km/h over the limit, regardless of the road

ch-speed-07.explanation: SVG Art. 90 para. 4(b) makes an excess of at least 50 km/h, on roads where the limit is at most 50 km/h, automatically a Raser offence under para. 3, carrying a mandatory sentencing range of one to four years' imprisonment. Germany has no equivalent fixed statutory km/h threshold with a mandatory minimum prison term for urban speeding — there it typically remains a fine/driving ban, with criminally relevant endangerment assessed case by case under StGB §§ 315c/315d.

ch-speed-08.question: Outside built-up areas the general speed limit is 80 km/h. From what amount over the limit does the Raser offence under SVG Art. 90 para. 4 automatically apply?

options.a: From 40 km/h over the limit
options.b: From 50 km/h over the limit
options.c: From 60 km/h over the limit
options.d: From 80 km/h over the limit

ch-speed-08.explanation: SVG Art. 90 para. 4(c) sets the threshold, on roads where the limit is at most 80 km/h, at an excess of at least 60 km/h — e.g. from 140 km/h on an ordinary 80 km/h rural road. The four graduated thresholds (40/50/60/80 km/h depending on road category) form a statutory scale with a mandatory minimum prison sentence as the legal consequence that has no equivalent in German road traffic law.

ch-speed-09.question: On a motorway (speed limit above 80 km/h), a driver is measured at least 80 km/h over the applicable limit. What consequence does SVG Art. 90 para. 3 impose?

options.a: Imprisonment of at least one year up to four years, as a Raser offence
options.b: Only a fixed penalty fine, because it happened on a motorway
options.c: A monetary penalty, but no prison sentence is provided for in law
options.d: The driving licence remains valid in every case, since it is only a risk to property

ch-speed-09.explanation: SVG Art. 90 para. 4(d) draws the line, on roads with a limit above 80 km/h, at an excess of at least 80 km/h; this automatically triggers para. 3's imprisonment range of one to four years, plus routinely a licence revocation and vehicle confiscation under SVG Art. 90a. A statutory mandatory minimum prison term for a speeding offence — combined with possible vehicle seizure — does not exist in German law; there, even extreme speeding usually remains an administrative or criminal matter without a fixed minimum sentence of this kind.

ch-speed-10.question: One driver exceeds the built-up-area speed limit by 8 km/h, another by 55 km/h. What is the basic difference in how they are fined?

options.a: Both pay the same fixed fine regardless of income
options.b: Both are punished exclusively by income-based day-fines
options.c: The 8 km/h case is settled with a flat, income-independent fixed penalty (Ordnungsbusse) under the OBV, while the 55 km/h case is a Raser offence punished with an income-scaled monetary penalty (Tagessätze) or imprisonment
options.d: Switzerland makes no distinction between a fixed penalty and a monetary penalty

ch-speed-10.explanation: Minor speeding is sanctioned under the Ordnungsbussenverordnung (OBV) with flat, income-independent fines (a few francs per km/h over). But once the Raser threshold of SVG Art. 90 para. 4 is reached — here, inside built-up areas, from 50 km/h over, so the 55 km/h case qualifies — the fixed penalty is replaced by a monetary penalty assessed in day-fines (Tagessätze, scaled to income) or imprisonment. Germany also has both fixed fines (Owi-Bussgeld) and day-fines, but lacks this sharp, statutorily fixed km/h threshold at which the system mandatorily switches from a flat fine to an income-scaled criminal penalty.

ch-vulnerable_users-01.question: At a stop without a bus bay, passengers are getting off a Postauto (public bus). What does SVG Art. 33 para. 3 require of other drivers?

options.a: They must show consideration for people boarding and alighting.
options.b: They must always stop and may only continue once the bus pulls away, as under Germany's § 20 StVO.
options.c: They may pass at unreduced speed, since the duty of consideration only applies at pedestrian crossings.
options.d: They must sound the horn to warn the passengers.

ch-vulnerable_users-01.explanation: SVG Art. 33 para. 3 only imposes a general duty of consideration toward boarding and alighting passengers, without spelling out exact conduct. This is one case where German law is stricter: § 20 StVO requires walking pace and a ban on passing buses or trams with hazard lights on until the doors are closed. Switzerland has no such specific rule at an ordinary stop.

ch-vulnerable_users-02.question: A pedestrian is standing right in front of a marked pedestrian crossing (Zebrastreifen) and clearly intends to cross. How must the driver behave under VRV Art. 6 para. 1?

options.a: Reduce speed in good time and stop if necessary to let her cross first.
options.b: Continue driving as long as she has not yet stepped onto the roadway.
options.c: Just sound the horn to warn her; stopping is not required.
options.d: Stop and only continue once she has left the entire crossing, regardless of the rest of the traffic situation.

ch-vulnerable_users-02.explanation: VRV Art. 6 para. 1 requires drivers to slow down before reaching the crossing and to yield to anyone clearly intending to cross, even before they step onto the road. German law (§ 26 StVO) ties the duty to yield more narrowly to people already on the crossing or clearly about to step onto it immediately.

ch-vulnerable_users-03.question: An unaccompanied blind pedestrian raises their white cane to cross the road away from a marked crossing. What does VRV Art. 6 para. 4 provide?

options.a: They must always be given the right of way.
options.b: The right of way only applies at a marked crossing; away from one, there is no specific white-cane rule, as in Germany.
options.c: They must be accompanied by another person, otherwise no right of way applies.
options.d: The right of way only applies during daytime, not at night.

ch-vulnerable_users-03.explanation: VRV Art. 6 para. 4 grants unaccompanied blind pedestrians who visibly raise the white cane absolute priority anywhere on the road, not just at a marked crossing. German law has no such explicit rule tied to the white cane; it relies instead on the StVO's general duty of care.

ch-vulnerable_users-04.question: A school bus is stopped with its hazard lights on and children are getting off. How may other vehicles pass it under VRV Art. 6 para. 5?

options.a: Only slowly and cautiously, stopping if necessary.
options.b: Only at an exact walking pace, as precisely defined under Germany's § 20 StVO.
options.c: Passing is prohibited outright; drivers must come to a full stop until the bus moves off again.
options.d: They may pass at normal speed as long as they sound the horn.

ch-vulnerable_users-04.explanation: VRV Art. 6 para. 5 only requires drivers passing a stopped school bus with hazard lights to go "slowly and cautiously", stopping if necessary — without the precise walking-pace figure or the strict no-passing rule that Germany's § 20 StVO imposes. Here too, German law is more precisely and strictly worded than Swiss law.

ch-vulnerable_users-05.question: Two cyclists want to ride side by side. What does VRV Art. 46 provide as the basic rule?

options.a: Riding side by side is prohibited in principle; only the Federal Council may allow exceptions.
options.b: Riding side by side is allowed as long as it does not obstruct anyone, as under Germany's § 2 para. 4 StVO.
options.c: Riding side by side is only prohibited on motorways, and permitted everywhere else.
options.d: Riding side by side is only prohibited after dark.

ch-vulnerable_users-05.explanation: VRV Art. 46 requires cyclists to ride in single file as the default rule; riding side by side needs a Federal Council exception. Germany went the opposite direction: since a 2020 amendment, § 2 para. 4 StVO permits riding side by side as long as other traffic is not obstructed — a clear difference from Switzerland.

ch-vulnerable_users-06.question: For lack of a sidewalk, a person is pushing a pram along the roadway. What does VRV Art. 48 require?

options.a: They must follow pedestrian rules, proceeding on the roadway in single file.
options.b: They must keep to the far right like a vehicle and follow the right-of-way rules for vehicles.
options.c: They may use the middle of the roadway, since prams have priority over all vehicles.
options.d: They must fit the pram with a warning light.

ch-vulnerable_users-06.explanation: VRV Art. 48 treats people pushing hand carts, prams, wheelchairs, or bicycles as pedestrians and explicitly requires them to walk in single file when on the roadway. German law has a comparable equal treatment with pedestrians (§ 25 StVO) but does not spell out such an explicit single-file formation.

ch-vulnerable_users-07.question: In a Begegnungszone ("encounter zone", sign 2.59.5), a pedestrian and a car meet. Who has the right of way under SSV Art. 22b, and what is the maximum speed?

options.a: The pedestrian has the right of way; the maximum speed is 20 km/h.
options.b: As in Germany's verkehrsberuhigter Bereich, only mutual consideration applies rather than a clear right of way, at walking pace.
options.c: The pedestrian has the right of way, but the maximum speed is 30 km/h as in an ordinary 30 km/h zone.
options.d: The driver generally has the right of way over pedestrians.

ch-vulnerable_users-07.explanation: SSV Art. 22b expressly gives pedestrians and users of vehicle-like devices priority over vehicles in a Begegnungszone and caps speed at 20 km/h. Germany has no direct equivalent: in a verkehrsberuhigter Bereich (sign 325.1), pedestrians may use the whole surface, but only mutual consideration at walking pace applies — the StVO does not expressly grant pedestrians the right of way there.

ch-vulnerable_users-08.question: A 6-year-old child (110 cm) is to ride in a Swiss taxi that has no child seat. What does VRV Art. 3a para. 4 provide?

options.a: The child must still be secured in a suitable restraint system; Swiss law has no general taxi exception like Germany's § 21 para. 1a StVO.
options.b: As in Germany, the child may exceptionally be secured with just the ordinary seatbelt because the taxi has no child seat.
options.c: Children aged 6 and over never need a restraint system in Switzerland anyway.
options.d: The child may ride without a restraint system if held on the lap of an accompanying adult in the front seat.

ch-vulnerable_users-08.explanation: VRV Art. 3a para. 4 requires a restraint system for children under 12 (or under 150 cm); the listed exceptions (150 cm, special seats from age 4, buses from age 4, lap-belt-only seats from age 7) do not mention taxis. Germany, by contrast, expressly allows in § 21 para. 1a sentence 4 StVO that a child in a taxi without a child seat be secured with the ordinary belt. The age/height threshold itself (12 years / 150 cm) is identical in both countries — the difference lies in this taxi exception.

ch-vulnerable_users-09.question: A slow e-bike (Leicht-Motorfahrrad with pedal assistance up to 25 km/h under VTS Art. 18) has been subject to a special rule under VRV Art. 30 para. 2 since 2022. What is it?

options.a: It must be ridden with its light switched on at all times, including in daylight.
options.b: Like an ordinary bicycle, it only needs a light in darkness or poor visibility, as with a German Pedelec 25.
options.c: It needs a yellow number plate like a fast e-bike.
options.d: A light is only required above 20 km/h, not below that speed.

ch-vulnerable_users-09.explanation: Since April 2022, VRV Art. 30 para. 2 has required all e-bikes to run with their lights on permanently, regardless of visibility conditions. An ordinary bicycle, and a German Pedelec 25, need a light only in darkness or poor visibility. A number plate is not required for the slow e-bike — that only applies to fast e-bikes.

ch-vulnerable_users-10.question: An e-bike with pedal assistance up to 45 km/h (a "fast Motorfahrrad" under VTS Art. 18) may only be ridden in Switzerland with...

options.a: a category M driving licence, a yellow number plate, and an approved safety helmet (not an ordinary bicycle helmet).
options.b: as in Germany, merely a moped test certificate and an ordinary bicycle helmet, with no number plate at all.
options.c: no licence at all, since e-bikes are generally treated like bicycles.
options.d: a category A (motorcycle) driving licence, but no number plate.

ch-vulnerable_users-10.explanation: A fast e-bike up to 45 km/h under VTS Art. 18 is no longer legally a bicycle: it requires a category M driving licence, a yellow number plate, and an approved safety helmet — an ordinary bicycle helmet is not enough. The slow e-bike up to 25 km/h needs none of this; there, a minimum age of 16 and no licence suffice. Germany requires a licence, insurance plate, and helmet for the comparable S-Pedelec too, but under a different system (plate colour rotates yearly instead of a fixed yellow, and licence class AM instead of M).
